narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. While the average accepted student ranked around the middle of their class, you placed in the bottom decile. This low standing signaled to the model a higher risk that you might struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. Both scores pulled the prediction toward passing. Your LSAT of 36 sits only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, and your 3.4 undergraduate GPA actually exceeds the 3.23 average of those who were admitted. These are solid achievements that helped your case.

Unfortunately, the impact of your third-year ranking outweighed the positive effects of your test scores and grades, resulting in the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance in the remaining law school years and consider a structured bar-preparation program. Improving your class rank and gaining bar-specific study experience could meaningfully lower your risk on a future application.
